title: Burns
why_this_matters: Burns in dogs are uncommon, and only small canine case series were retrieved; heat-related burns can follow sun exposure in hot weather and can accompany heat exhaustion or heatstroke [1].

what_changes_from_human.point: A dog's coat can hide burns: in 16 dogs with sun-related dorsal burns, lesions were alopecia, erythema, ulcers, eschar and crusts on the back, mostly in dark, short-coated dogs in hot months [1].
Signs of heat exhaustion or heatstroke preceded the skin lesions in 4 of 16 dogs, so treat a burned dog from hot weather as a possible heat illness patient too (see the heat stroke module) [1].

recognition: Dorsal thermal necrosis: 15 of 16 cases occurred May to September in the southwestern USA; histology matched partial and full-thickness thermal burns [1].
Most were treated supportively with analgesics and antimicrobials; most healed by second intention and 2 dogs had surgery [1].

management: TODO: first aid for an acute thermal burn in a dog. No canine source retrieved. The reviewer decides scope; do not adapt human burn protocols.

One nine-case series (5 dogs, 4 cats) reported healing with a vitamin-supplemented medical-grade honey product, but it was small, uncontrolled and some authors are affiliated with the product maker [2]. Not a recommendation.

takeaway: A dog burned by sun, fire or hot surfaces needs a veterinarian; check for heat illness and smoke inhalation too.
